messages:
meena: Pushed a small benchmark summary comparing streaming (SSE/WebSocket) vs non-streaming HTTP endpoints across regions and GPU types. TL;DR: streaming wins p50 latency at low concurrency but non-streaming gives better sustained throughput on A100/H100 when batching is enabled. charts + raw results here: https://redwood-internal.s3/bench/1766601123

chris: Thanks — can you paste the main numbers inline? quick skim of the pdf is slow.

meena: Sure. High-level numbers from eu-west-1 (H100) and us-east-1 (A100):
- single-request p50 (streaming SSE): H100 ~ 18ms, A100 ~ 26ms
- single-request p50 (non-streaming, no batching): H100 ~ 22ms, A100 ~ 30ms
- sustained throughput tokens/s per GPU (packed batching, batch size ~ 16): H100 non-stream ~ 380k tok/s, H100 streaming ~ 310k tok/s
- A100 non-stream ~ 240k tok/s, A100 streaming ~ 200k tok/s

alex: Interesting. So streaming lower p50 but hurts peak tokens/sec when batching. What's p99 behavior?

meena: p99 for streaming is spikier due to event loop wakeups and per-connection overhead when many concurrent clients hold open streams. For H100 in eu-west-1 at 128 concurrent clients:
- SSE p99 ~ 420ms (when we hit backpressure briefly)
- WebSocket p99 ~ 380ms
- HTTP non-stream p99 (batched) ~ 210ms

sam: Did you test int8 vs int4 quantized kernels? I remember the quantized kernels on A100 behave oddly with streaming.

meena: Yes — ran quantization sweep. Key points:
- int8 (q8) preserves quality and gives ~1.25x throughput vs fp16 for non-stream batched workloads.
- int4 (q4) increases throughput further (~1.6x) but introduced a tiny regression on long-context perplexity for the model we tested.
- On H100, the int4 kernel currently falls back more often to the generic matmul path under streaming (small seq-len variance), causing p99 spikes. So int4 + streaming = unpredictable latency spikes.

perf-bot: [AUTO] Collected metrics for run 1766601123: samples=12, median_latency_ms=24, p99_latency_ms=410, tokens_sec=312000, region=eu-west-1, gpu=H100, mode=streaming

chris: Good to have that bot line. What about region differences? APAC?

meena: APAC (ap-southeast-1) numbers were ~8-12% worse in p50 due to slightly older instance types and network tail. Throughput per GPU similar after accounting for instance SKU (we used A100s in US/EU, and A40-equivalent in APAC). The real diff was network RTT; streaming sessions pay more on RTT because of more frequent event roundtrips.

alex: Any kernel-level notes? Which kernels were dominant for streaming vs non-streaming?

meena: Yes. Kernel selection notes:
- Non-streaming (batched) favors large GEMM kernels and fused attention kernels (fast path). Kernel scheduler packs sequences into dense batches and uses cuBLAS/cuDNN tuned kernels.
- Streaming favors smaller per-token attention kernels and optimized KV cache paths. On H100 we hit a specialized attention kernel that is great for single-token regen but falls back on CUDA generic kernels when sequence-length distribution varies, which hurts p99.

sam: How do these findings affect capacity sizing and routing? e.g., should we prefer dedicated non-stream endpoints for high-throughput batch jobs and streaming endpoints for interactive low-concurrency UX?

meena: That's the recommended pattern:
- Interactive apps with low concurrency, strict p50: use streaming (SSE/WebSocket), prefer H100 and q8 if quality acceptable.
- High sustained throughput / inference pipelines: prefer non-streaming HTTP with aggressive batching and quantized kernels (q8 or q4 if evals pass). Batch size tuning is critical.
- For region routing: route latency-sensitive clients in-region to streaming endpoints; for bulk jobs, route to cheaper regions (with same SKU) and use non-streaming batching.

alex: Any config hints for streaming to reduce p99 spikes?

meena: A few operational knobs we used in the experiments:
- per-connection write window: increase to reduce small-write syscall overhead
- event loop pinning: pin streaming workers to a dedicated core to reduce thread contention
- prefix/KV caching: aggressively enable across clients to cut repeated compute for similar prompts
- backpressure policy: favor shedding new requests when GPU queue > X instead of keeping streams open indefinitely

chris: Did you test SSE vs WebSocket differences specifically?

meena: SSE and WebSocket latency profiles were close; WebSocket slightly better on p99 in heavily concurrent tests because it reuses a single TCP connection more efficiently on certain infra. SSE is simpler to operate and works great behind HTTP LB with standard healthchecks. Choose WebSocket if you expect many small messages from client.

sam: Action items?

meena: Drafted recommendations at the bottom of the report:
1) Default for new interactive customers: streaming on H100 with q8 kernels, enable prefix caching.
2) Default for bulk customers: non-streaming endpoints w/ batching, prefer q8, offer q4 as opt-in after evals.
3) Create a small runbook for streaming p99 mitigation (pin worker, write window, backpressure).
4) Follow-up experiment: H100 int4 kernel fix is in PR #834 — re-run after merge to see if streaming p99 improves.

alex: Cool. Can you add the 95/99th percentile distributions (histograms) to the S3 folder so infra can consume them for autoscaler tuning?

meena: Done — uploaded histograms and per-client traces to https://redwood-internal.s3/bench/1766601123/traces/ (jsonl + csv).
